In our last article, Google and Samsung take on Dolby Atmos, with a little help from aespa, we mentioned that someone is gunning for Dolby’s place in spatial sound. This time, let’s take a proper look at spatial sound itself.

Spatial sound, also called immersive sound or 3D sound, is a transformative audio technology. It creates a three-dimensional listening experience in which sound seems to arrive from every direction: in front, behind, above, below and all around. Its aim is to reproduce the way humans naturally hear in three-dimensional space. By simulating the direction, distance and movement of sounds, it creates an immersive audio experience.

In everyday life, when we hear a sound, the brain uses information from our two ears (shaped by our head and ears) to work out its direction, distance and source. Spatial sound technology mimics this natural hearing process, usually with advanced algorithms and hardware, to create an immersive sound field.

Key features of spatial sound

  1. Directionality: sounds can be placed in any direction, including above, below and all around, mirroring the way we hear sounds coming from every side.
  2. Distance: sounds can be rendered so that the listener senses how near or far they are, adding depth and layering.
  3. Movement: sounds can change dynamically, creating the sense that they are moving.
  4. Height: sounds can come from above or below, adding further realism.

How does spatial sound work?

Creating spatial sound takes a combination of hardware and software that imitates how we naturally process sound. Together they use timing, intensity and the way each of our two ears receives sound to build a convincing sonic space.

Key technologies behind spatial sound

  1. Head-related transfer functions (HRTFs): an HRTF describes how sound is filtered by the shape of the ears and head, which is what helps us locate where a sound comes from. Spatial sound algorithms use HRTF data to reproduce how we naturally perceive sounds arriving from different angles. Source positions are computed from these cues, creating a realistic three-dimensional sound space.
  2. Binaural audio: binaural recording uses two microphones placed to mimic the positions of the human ears, capturing how sound interacts with the head and body. Played back over headphones, a binaural recording conveys a realistic sense of space and direction. It is widely used in virtual reality, ASMR content and immersive audio recordings.
  3. Multichannel audio systems: surround formats such as 5.1 and 7.1, and advanced systems such as Dolby Atmos, surround the listener with multiple loudspeakers to simulate a three-dimensional sound environment. Dolby Atmos, for example, goes beyond conventional surround loudspeakers and adds ceiling speakers for height, so sound can come from above and below, deepening the sense of immersion.
  4. Software algorithms: advanced software processing plays a crucial role in simulating spatial sound. Algorithms place and move sounds in three-dimensional space, adjusting their level, pitch and delay according to the listener’s position and orientation. This makes audio in virtual environments and games far more dynamic and interactive.

Applications of spatial sound

Spatial sound is transforming a number of industries by changing how we interact with audio. It has become essential in virtual reality, gaming, film, music production and more. Here are some of the most important areas where it is used:

1. Virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR)

In VR and AR, spatial sound is a key ingredient of an immersive experience. It helps users feel that they are truly “there” in the virtual world, with sound seeming to come from all around them. In a VR game, for instance, spatial sound helps players locate enemies, interact with virtual objects and become fully absorbed in the environment. Without it, VR would feel more detached and less real.

2. Gaming

In video games, spatial sound heightens realism by letting players hear their surroundings through a full 360 degrees. This is especially useful in first-person shooters (FPS), survival games and adventure games, where accurate sound localization is crucial to gameplay. Players can clearly hear footsteps, gunfire or distant explosions, for example, which makes for a better gaming experience.

3. Film and home theater

Spatial sound systems such as Dolby Atmos and DTS:X have revolutionized how we experience films and TV shows. They let sound surround the audience in three-dimensional space, creating a sense of immersion that conventional stereo or surround systems could not achieve. In an action scene, for example, the audience can hear an aircraft roar overhead, debris rain down all around, or objects whoosh past from the side, all of which add to the excitement and immersion.

4. Music production and live concerts

In music production, spatial sound can create a more immersive listening experience by placing instruments and vocals in a three-dimensional sound space. Artists and producers can explore new approaches to mixing and arrangement that add a sense of depth. Concerts and live performances have also begun to use spatial sound technology to enhance the audience’s experience, so that the music reaches them from every direction.

5. Hearing devices and assistive technology

Spatial sound technology is also used in hearing devices such as hearing aids, helping users better locate the sounds around them. By improving directionality, these devices help people with hearing loss hear their surroundings more naturally and take part more fully in conversations and activities.

Benefits of spatial sound

1. Greater immersion

The main benefit of spatial sound is that it deepens the listener’s sense of immersion. In VR, games and films, this added realism makes users feel they are actually “inside” a virtual world rather than merely watching it.

2. Better sound localization

Spatial sound improves how accurately listeners can judge the direction and distance of sounds. Accurate localization is critical in gaming, in emergencies and in some medical applications.

3. More engagement

By simulating a three-dimensional sound space, spatial sound draws listeners further into the content and increases their engagement. That is why it is so effective in VR and gaming, where users’ attention and immersion are paramount.

4. A more natural sound

Spatial sound brings audio closer to the way our auditory system naturally processes it, doing away with the flat, two-dimensional presentation of conventional stereo and making listening more organic and vivid.

Spatial sound (or immersive sound) marks a major step forward in audio. By simulating the way the human brain naturally processes hearing, it lets us perceive sound in three-dimensional space, deepening immersion and engagement in VR, gaming, film, music and beyond. As the technology keeps developing, spatial sound has the potential to redefine how we perceive and interact with digital spaces, bringing a new level of realism and connection.


Major Chinese music streaming platforms such as QQ Music and NetEase Cloud Music already offer spatial audio, but only as a paid add-on, at about 10 yuan (roughly US$1.40) a month. So here’s our question: would you pay extra for spatial audio? Or do you think that in the long run it will end up free? Let us know what you think in the comments.
